Some of a tool’s failures are flaky network timeouts; others are malformed inputs that will never succeed. What is the right error-handling split?

practice: Retry transient timeouts automatically inside the tool, but return syntax errors immediately with clear validation details so the agent can self-correct.
Absorb network retries in the backend; surface input-validation failures to the agent right away with specifics.
timed: Handle timeout retries within the tool’s own logic and hand syntax errors straight back to the agent with explicit validation detail for correction.

practice: Pass all errors to the agent and prompt it to retry timeouts but stop on syntax errors.
timed: Surface every error and instruct the agent on which kind to retry.
Let the agent triage all failures per prompt guidance.

practice: Uniformly auto-retry every error 3 times before returning a failure message.
timed: Retry all failures three times regardless of type.
Apply a blanket 3-retry policy to every error class.

practice: Return all errors immediately as a generic "Tool Execution Failed" message.
timed: Report every failure with the same generic error string.
Send back an undifferentiated failure message for all errors.

d4-010.explanation: Agents should not spend context and turns resolving predictable system-level failures — transient timeouts belong in an engineering retry loop inside the tool. Syntax errors need the agent’s reasoning to fix the input, so return them immediately with explicit validation details. Pushing retry loops to the LLM wastes turns; retrying a malformed input fails identically three times; generic messages give the model nothing to correct against.

stem: An extract_metadata tool returns a DOI that the lookup_citations and verify_doi tools require. When users ask to "extract the metadata and tell me how cited it is," the model sometimes calls the enrichment tools first and they fail. What most reliably enforces the order?
Two enrichment tools depend on a DOI produced by an extraction tool, but the model occasionally invokes them before extraction has run. What is the most dependable fix?

practice: Force extract_metadata on the first turn via tool_choice, then switch to tool_choice "auto" for subsequent turns.
Use a forced tool_choice for the prerequisite extraction call, releasing to "auto" once the DOI is in context.
timed: Set tool_choice to require the extraction tool on turn one, then relax to "auto" so the enrichment tools can run with the DOI available.

practice: Add a prompt instruction to always call extract_metadata first.
timed: State the required ordering explicitly in the prompt.
Instruct the model in the system prompt to extract before enriching.

practice: Combine all three tools into a single tool that does everything.
timed: Merge extraction and enrichment into one combined tool.
Collapse the three tools into a single all-in-one call.

practice: Keep tool_choice on "auto" but reword the enrichment tools’ descriptions to discourage early use.
timed: Leave selection automatic and soften the enrichment descriptions.
Rely on "auto" selection with descriptions warning against early calls.

d4-011.explanation: When tools have a strict dependency, enforce it deterministically: force the prerequisite tool with tool_choice on the first turn, then release to "auto" once its output is in context. Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate; merging the tools destroys composability; under "auto" the model may still attempt the second step regardless of description wording.

stem: An extraction system uses a 12-field schema and tool descriptions totaling ~2,500 tokens on a 200k-context model. Documents under 150k tokens extract at 98% accuracy, but 175k-185k documents drop to 71%, with the final third of the document consistently missing. What is the most likely cause?

On a 200k-window model, extraction accuracy collapses only for documents near 180k tokens, and it is specifically end-of-document content that goes missing; the schema and system prompt add a few thousand tokens of input. Why?

practice: The tool definition and system prompt consume input tokens, pushing the total near the context limit, where attention over end-of-prompt content degrades.
Schema plus system-prompt tokens shrink the effective document space; near the absolute limit, attention on the final content deteriorates.
timed: The fixed schema and prompt overhead put long documents close to the hard context boundary, and attention degrades for content at the end of a near-limit prompt.

practice: Schemas exceeding 8-10 fields inherently increase decision complexity and reduce accuracy.
timed: Twelve fields is past the complexity threshold where extraction degrades.
The field count alone makes the schema too complex to fill accurately.

practice: Very long documents exceed the model’s effective attention span, causing middle-of-document degradation.
timed: It is the lost-in-the-middle effect on long documents.
Long inputs degrade in the middle, which is what is being observed.

practice: The model distributes attention proportionally across the input, starving the end of the document.
timed: Attention is spread evenly, so the ending gets proportionally too little.
Proportional attention allocation leaves the final section under-attended.

d5-001.explanation: Context limits are absolute: ~4k tokens of schema and system prompt shrink a 200k window to ~196k of document space, and payloads approaching the boundary suffer degraded end-of-prompt attention — matching the "final third missing" symptom. Schema complexity causes wrong values, not positional omission (the same schema scores 98% on short docs); lost-in-the-middle affects the middle, not the end; proportional attention distribution is a fabricated concept.

stem: Asynchronous requests carry a strict 30-hour SLA from submission to result. You use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours per batch. Which submission schedule meets the SLA at the lowest cost?
With a 30-hour result SLA and batches that may take the full 24 hours to process, how often should you submit batches to stay compliant while minimizing orchestration cost?

practice: Every 6 hours — the longest interval where worst-case wait plus 24h processing still fits the 30-hour SLA.
Submit on a 6-hour cadence: a request waits at most 6h, so 6h + 24h processing equals exactly the 30h bound with the fewest batches.
timed: On a 6-hour schedule, since interval + 24h processing must stay within 30h and 6h is the largest interval that satisfies it.

practice: Every 4 hours, keeping a comfortable margin under the SLA.
timed: Submit every 4 hours for buffer below the 30-hour limit.
Use a 4-hour cadence so worst case lands at 28 hours.

practice: One large batch at the end of each day.
timed: Batch everything up daily and submit once every 24 hours.
Submit a single daily batch to minimize submissions.

practice: Switch to the synchronous API to guarantee the SLA.
timed: Abandon batching and process requests synchronously for SLA safety.
Use the real-time API so results always arrive in time.

d5-002.explanation: Worst case = submission interval + 24h max processing, and it must not exceed 30h, so the interval must be ≤ 6h. Six hours is the longest compliant interval — fewest batches, lowest orchestration cost. Every 4 hours also meets the SLA but submits more batches than necessary for the stated cost goal; a daily batch yields 24h + 24h = 48h and blows the SLA; synchronous processing forfeits the 50% batch discount.

stem: A pipeline resends a 40-page policy document as context on every one of thousands of calls. Latency and cost are high; the document rarely changes. What is the best fix?
Thousands of calls each prepend the same large, rarely-changing document. Cost and latency are the complaint. Which change helps most?

practice: Apply prompt caching (cache_control) to the static document prefix so it is not reprocessed each call.
Mark the unchanging prefix with a cache breakpoint to reuse it across calls.
timed: Set a cache_control breakpoint on the stable prefix so repeated context is served from cache.

practice: Switch the whole pipeline to the smallest model to cut cost.
timed: Move everything to the cheapest model tier.
Downgrade the entire pipeline to the smallest model.

practice: Truncate the document to its first page on every call.
timed: Send only the first page of the document each time.
Clip the document to page one for every request.

practice: Request a rate-limit increase to push more calls through.
timed: Ask for higher rate limits to raise throughput.
Get the rate limit bumped to send more calls.

d5-003.explanation: A large, static, frequently-reused prefix is the textbook prompt-caching case - cache_control cuts latency and cost without losing context. Downgrading the model risks quality, truncation loses information, and a rate-limit bump addresses throughput not the per-call waste. Judgment: match the fix to the actual cost driver.

stem: A RAG bot indexes each 50-page document as one chunk and stuffs the top 5 whole documents into the prompt. Answers are vague and miss specifics. What is the core fix?
A retrieval system uses whole 50-page documents as single chunks; responses are unfocused and lose detail. Which change addresses the root cause?

practice: Chunk documents into smaller, semantically coherent passages and retrieve/rank those, so the relevant specifics surface.
Split documents into focused passages and retrieve at passage granularity.
timed: Index smaller, meaning-coherent chunks and retrieve those passages instead of whole documents.

practice: Retrieve more whole documents per query.
timed: Pull back additional full documents each query.
Increase the number of whole documents retrieved.

practice: Raise the temperature so answers are more specific.
timed: Increase temperature to sharpen specificity.
Turn temperature up for more detailed answers.

practice: Switch to a larger-context model and keep whole-document chunks.
timed: Adopt a bigger context window and retain full-document chunks.
Use a larger-context model without re-chunking.

d5-004.explanation: Whole-document chunks bury the relevant passage and dilute retrieval; the core fix is smaller, semantically coherent chunks ranked at passage level. Retrieving more whole docs worsens dilution, temperature does not add precision, and a bigger context still feeds the model unfocused chunks.

stem: A pipeline produced 120k tokens of raw web content, 15k tokens of extracted insights, and a 3k-token synthesis narrative. The final report agent must now generate output with proper citations. What should the coordinator pass it?

Handing off to a report-generation agent that must cite sources, you can pass anything from the full 120k tokens of raw research down to just the 3k synthesis narrative. Which hand-off balances completeness and efficiency?

practice: The synthesis narrative plus a lean, structured citation index (claim, source, key quote per citation id) and any conflict flags.
The 3k narrative backbone together with a compact structured index of citation metadata and flagged conflicts.
timed: The narrative plus a small structured citation index — id, claim, source, key quote — and conflict flags, with raw content stripped.

practice: The 120k tokens of raw content along with all intermediate outputs, for completeness.
timed: Everything — raw research, intermediate analysis, and the narrative.
The full raw corpus plus every intermediate artifact.

practice: Only the 3k-token synthesis narrative, keeping the hand-off minimal.
timed: Just the narrative by itself for maximum efficiency.
The synthesis text alone, nothing else.

practice: The synthesis narrative plus the document-analysis agent’s full reasoning chain.
timed: The narrative along with the upstream agent’s complete reasoning trace.
The narrative accompanied by the full intermediate reasoning chain.

d5-005.explanation: Passing 135k+ tokens invites lost-in-the-middle degradation and wastes budget, while the bare narrative leaves the report agent no citation data — it will fabricate sources. The balance is the dense narrative plus a compact structured citation index carrying only essential metadata. Upstream reasoning chains are internal to the previous agent and add noise, not citations.

stem: Under load, a service receives 429 and 529 responses and immediately retries in a tight loop, which makes the overload worse. What is the right handling?
When the API returns 429/529 errors, an app retries instantly and repeatedly, amplifying the overload. Which approach is correct?

practice: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, respect any retry-after hint, and cap the number of attempts.
Back off exponentially with jitter, honor retry-after, and bound retries.
timed: Use capped exponential backoff with jitter and respect the retry-after header instead of immediate retries.

practice: Retry immediately and more aggressively to get through sooner.
timed: Retry faster and harder to push past the limit.
Hammer retries immediately to break through.

practice: Ignore the errors and silently drop the affected requests.
timed: Swallow the errors and discard those requests.
Suppress the 429/529s and drop the calls.

practice: Switch to a different model on every 429 response.
timed: Change models each time a 429 occurs.
Hop to another model on every rate-limit error.

d5-006.explanation: Rate-limit/overload errors call for capped exponential backoff with jitter and respect for retry-after. Immediate aggressive retries worsen the overload; dropping requests loses work silently; swapping models per 429 is a non-fix that ignores the throttling signal.

stem: A 10,000-document batch completes with 300 failures (3%) due to context_length_exceeded, each identified by its custom_id in the result file. What is the most cost-effective way to process the failures?
After a large batch run, 3% of documents failed with context-length errors; the result file maps each failure to a custom_id. How should you handle them at lowest cost?

practice: Extract only the 300 failed documents via their custom_id, chunk them to fit the context limit, and resubmit them as a new batch.
Isolate the failures with custom_id, split the oversized documents into smaller segments, and submit just those in a fresh batch.
timed: Use the custom_id mapping to pull out just the failures, chunk those documents down to size, and re-batch only them.

practice: Resubmit all 10,000 documents with a smaller chunk size.
timed: Re-run the entire batch with reduced chunking.
Redo the full 10,000-document run using smaller chunks.

practice: Switch the 300 failed documents to the synchronous API.
timed: Process the failures through the real-time API instead.
Send the failed documents synchronously to get them done.

practice: Increase the context window limit so the failures fit.
timed: Raise the model’s context limit to accommodate the documents.
Configure a larger context window for the oversized documents.

d5-007.explanation: Resubmitting everything pays again for the 97% that already succeeded. custom_id exists precisely to isolate failures: pull the 300, chunk them (the error means they exceed the context limit as-is), and re-batch. The synchronous API costs roughly double the batch rate and still requires the same chunking; context limits are fixed model constraints, not configurable settings.

stem: A pipeline has a complex multi-constraint planning step that produces shallow, error-prone output and a trivial formatting step that is fine. Where should you spend an extended-thinking budget?
Given one hard reasoning step and one simple formatting step, where is extended thinking worth enabling?

practice: Enable extended thinking on the hard multi-constraint reasoning step, not the trivial formatting step.
Spend the thinking budget on the complex planning step and skip it on formatting.
timed: Turn on extended thinking only for the demanding reasoning step, leaving the simple step without it.

practice: Enable it on every step for consistency.
timed: Apply thinking uniformly to all steps.
Switch it on everywhere for consistency.

practice: Avoid extended thinking entirely to keep costs down.
timed: Never use thinking, to minimize cost.
Disable it across the board for savings.

practice: Enable it on the formatting step, since output quality matters most there.
timed: Put the thinking budget on the formatting step.
Use extended thinking for the formatting work.

d5-008.explanation: Extended thinking pays off on genuinely hard reasoning, so spend it on the multi-constraint planning step and not the trivial one. Enabling it everywhere wastes cost/latency, banning it leaves the hard step weak, and putting it on formatting targets the step that does not need it.

stem: An extraction system ran 3 months with 100% human review; extractions at >=90% model confidence show 97% accuracy overall. Before automating those high-confidence extractions, what validation step is most critical?
You plan to stop human review for extractions above a 90% confidence score, since their aggregate accuracy is 97%. What must you check before deploying the automation?

practice: Segment the accuracy metrics by document type and field — an aggregate 97% can hide catastrophic failure rates in specific subsets.
Run a stratified analysis breaking accuracy down per document type and per field before removing humans from any segment.
timed: Break the 97% down by document type and field first, since the aggregate can mask badly failing categories that still need review.

practice: Deploy the automation globally at the >=90% confidence threshold, since the data supports it.
timed: Ship the threshold as-is — three months of data is sufficient evidence.
Roll it out everywhere at 90% confidence given the measured accuracy.

practice: Run a random-sample review across all documents before deploying.
timed: Spot-check a random sample of documents as the final gate.
Validate with one random sampling pass over the corpus.

practice: Raise the confidence threshold to >=95% as a safety margin.
timed: Bump the cutoff to 95% confidence to be safe.
Tighten the threshold to 95% before automating.

d5-009.explanation: Aggregate accuracy is dangerous: 97% overall can coexist with, say, 61% on handwritten forms. Stratifying by document type and field ensures automation only removes humans from segments that are actually safe. Deploying on the aggregate silently ships high error rates for edge categories; random sampling under-represents rare document types; raising the threshold still trusts self-reported confidence, which is an unreliable accuracy proxy.
